lead: A composite is two materials that stay separate but work as a team. One, the matrix, holds the shape, spreads the load and shields the other from water, air and rubbing. The other, the reinforcement, is stiff and strong and carries most of the load. Alone each is ordinary. Joined, the pair gives far more stiffness and strength per kilogram than the matrix alone, and more than a metal part of the same weight — though never more than the bare fibre along its own axis. Boat hulls, wind-turbine blades, cricket-bat handles, brake discs and cutting tools are composites. This chapter covers what each part does, the main families, how they are made, and the one formula you must be able to use.
prereq: You need: 5.5 for how packing decides stiffness and density, and 5.6 for epoxy and polyester resins.

sections.h3: The two parts and the bond between them

blocks.text: A composite has two materials that do not dissolve into each other. The matrix is the continuous phase: it holds the reinforcement in place, hands load from one fibre to the next, and shields the fibre from water, air and rubbing. The reinforcement is the dispersed phase — fibres, whiskers or particles stiffer and stronger than the matrix. The matrix alone is weak; loose fibre cannot be shaped or protected. Together they make a part far better than the matrix alone.

Load enters the fibre only through the interface. Pull the composite and the matrix shears, passing stress to the fibre surface. A coupling agent such as a silane on glass improves this grip. A weak bond lets fibres slide out — pull-out — and the part fails far below the fibre's own strength. A bond that is too stiff makes the part brittle: nothing slides, so nothing absorbs energy. Good design wants a bond strong enough to carry load and weak enough to let fibres debond and bridge a growing crack.

items: Continuous fibre: long and aligned, load carried along the length; stiffest along the axis.
Chopped or woven fibre: short or interlaced, drapes over a mould, lower stiffness.
Particulate: powder or flakes; raises hardness and wear resistance, carries little tensile load.

blocks.text: A laminate is not a fibre form: it is a way of stacking plies at chosen angles, so the plate can be stiff in the directions you pick — a cross-ply laminate in two, a quasi-isotropic one in all in-plane directions.

sections.h3: Polymer matrix composites and how they are made

blocks.text: The matrix is a resin, usually epoxy or polyester (5.6). Polymer matrix composites lead the market because they are light — 1.5 to 2.0 g/cm³ — and cure at room temperature. Their weakness is heat: epoxy matrices soften or degrade near 120–150 °C and polyester well below that, so a polymer matrix composite stays away from exhausts and furnaces.

items: Glass (E-glass): cheapest; E<sub>f</sub> ≈ 70 GPa, density 2.5 g/cm³, insulating; water tanks, boat hulls, circuit boards.

Carbon: E<sub>f</sub> 230–600 GPa, density ≈ 1.8 g/cm³, conducts electricity, costly; aircraft panels, bicycle frames, and the handles and toe guards of some cricket bats (the blade itself is willow).
Aramid: very tough, density ≈ 1.45 g/cm³, weak in compression; helmets, ropes, bullet-resistant vests.
Hand lay-up: glass mat laid in an open mould, resin brushed in, cured in air. Cheap and slow, one smooth face, plenty of labour. Boat hulls and water tanks.
Pultrusion: continuous tows pulled through a resin bath and then a heated die. Constant cross-section only — rods, ladders, cable trays.
Resin transfer moulding: dry fibre preform sealed in a closed mould, resin pumped in under pressure. Two smooth faces, controlled fibre fraction, less styrene vapour. Blade parts and car panels.

blocks.text: Ceramics stay hard to 1000 °C and beyond, but one crack shatters them. A ceramic matrix composite puts ceramic fibres in a ceramic matrix; as a crack opens, fibres bridge it and pull out, absorbing energy. The part does not become ductile — it becomes damage tolerant.

items: SiC–SiC: silicon carbide fibres in a silicon carbide matrix. Made by chemical vapour infiltration, where a chloride gas seeps into the fibre preform and deposits SiC, or by hot pressing. Turbine shrouds, heat shields and high-performance car brake discs. (Aircraft brakes are carbon–carbon, a different family.)
Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>–SiC: alumina with silicon carbide whiskers, hot pressed into cutting tool inserts that run hot and fast.

blocks.text: Hot pressing gives dense, simple shapes; infiltration gives complex shapes with some porosity left. Both cost far more than a polymer composite, so ceramics go only where hardness or heat decides the sale.

Pull a unidirectional composite along its fibres and fibre and matrix stretch by the same amount, so the load is shared in proportion to stiffness. The composite stiffness is the volume-weighted average of the two.

blocks.where: E<sub>c</sub> is the composite modulus along the fibres (GPa); V<sub>f</sub> and V<sub>m</sub> are the volume fractions of fibre and matrix, with V<sub>f</sub> + V<sub>m</sub> = 1; E<sub>f</sub> and E<sub>m</sub> are the moduli of fibre and matrix (GPa).
ρ<sub>c</sub> is composite density and ρ<sub>f</sub>, ρ<sub>m</sub> are fibre and matrix densities, all in g/cm³; the same volume weighting applies.

blocks.text: Divide stiffness by density to get the specific modulus, Ec ÷ ρc, in GPa per g/cm³. This number, not stiffness alone, decides whether a part is worth its weight.

items: Holds for continuous, aligned fibres, loaded along the axis, with a good bond and equal strain.
Across the fibres the modulus is far lower, and this rule does not apply there.
Short or random fibres fall below the prediction; the rule is an upper bound for them.
V<sub>f</sub> above about 0.65 leaves too little resin to wet and hold the fibres.

examples.question: A unidirectional glass fibre–epoxy lamina has fibre volume fraction V<sub>f</sub> = 0.60. E-glass has E<sub>f</sub> = 70 GPa and ρ<sub>f</sub> = 2.5 g/cm³; the epoxy has E<sub>m</sub> = 3.5 GPa and ρ<sub>m</sub> = 1.2 g/cm³. Find (i) the modulus along the fibres, (ii) the density, and (iii) the specific modulus, comparing it with epoxy alone.
steps: Modulus along the fibres: E<sub>c</sub> = V<sub>f</sub>E<sub>f</sub> + V<sub>m</sub>E<sub>m</sub> = 0.60 × 70 + 0.40 × 3.5 = 42 + 1.4 = 43.4 GPa.
Specific modulus of the composite: 43.4 ÷ 1.98 = 21.9 GPa per g/cm³.
Epoxy alone: 3.5 ÷ 1.2 = 2.9 GPa per g/cm³. The composite is about 7.5 times stiffer per kilogram.
examples.answer: E<sub>c</sub> = 43.4 GPa, ρ<sub>c</sub> = 1.98 g/cm³ and specific modulus 21.9 GPa per g/cm³, against 2.9 for epoxy alone.
examples.check:
Ef = 70.0
Em = 3.5
Vf = 0.60
Vm = 1 - Vf
rho_f = 2.5
rho_m = 1.2
Ec = Vf*Ef + Vm*Em
rho_c = Vf*rho_f + Vm*rho_m
sm = Ec/rho_c
sm_e = Em/rho_m
print(round(Ec, 2))
print(round(rho_c, 2))
print(round(sm, 1))
print(round(sm_e, 1))

traps: Volume fraction, not weight fraction. V<sub>f</sub> + V<sub>m</sub> = 1 by volume; feeding weight percentages into the rule of mixtures gives a wrong modulus.
The rule of mixtures is for continuous aligned fibres loaded along the axis. Across the fibres, or for a chopped-strand mat, it overestimates stiffness badly.
Composite density is a weighted average and always lies between the two densities — never their sum, and never the fibre density alone.
A ceramic matrix composite gains damage tolerance, not ductility. It still does not yield and stretch like a metal.
Pultrusion makes a constant cross-section only. A part whose section changes needs resin transfer moulding or lay-up.

quiz.q: Define matrix and reinforcement in a composite.
quiz.a: The matrix is the continuous phase that holds the reinforcement, transfers load and protects it. The reinforcement is the dispersed phase — fibre, whisker or particle — that is stiffer and stronger and carries most of the load.

quiz.q: Name the three fibres commonly used in polymer matrix composites and give one use of each.
quiz.a: Glass: water tanks, boat hulls, circuit boards. Carbon: aircraft panels, bicycle frames. Aramid: helmets, ropes, bullet-resistant vests.

quiz.q: Why does a very weak fibre–matrix bond lower the strength of a composite?
quiz.a: Load reaches the fibre only through the interface. If the bond is weak, the matrix cannot shear stress into the fibre, so fibres pull out and the part fails at a load far below the fibre strength.

quiz.q: A unidirectional carbon–epoxy lamina has V<sub>f</sub> = 0.50, E<sub>f</sub> = 230 GPa, E<sub>m</sub> = 3.5 GPa, ρ<sub>f</sub> = 1.8 g/cm³ and ρ<sub>m</sub> = 1.2 g/cm³. Find E<sub>c</sub>, ρ<sub>c</sub> and the specific modulus.
Why does the rule of mixtures overestimate the modulus of a randomly oriented fibre mat?
quiz.a: The rule assumes every fibre is aligned with the load and shares the same strain. In a random mat most fibres lie at an angle, so they carry less of the load and the ones across the pull contribute almost nothing; the measured modulus falls well below the prediction.

quiz.q: A sliding part must run at 900 °C under load. Choose a polymer or a ceramic matrix composite and justify the choice.
quiz.a: Ceramic matrix composite. Epoxy matrices soften or degrade near 120–150 °C and polyester well below that, so neither can survive 900 °C. A CMC such as SiC–SiC keeps its hardness at that temperature and its fibres bridge cracks, so it tolerates damage instead of shattering.

beyond: Not for the exam. Wind-turbine blades are now moulded in one shot by vacuum-assisted resin infusion, with fibre angles chosen ply by ply. Hydrogen storage tanks are made by winding carbon fibre wetted with epoxy over a polymer liner. Ceramic matrix composites have entered jet engine turbine sections, where they replace nickel alloys and allow higher running temperatures. Thermoplastic composites such as carbon fibre in PEEK can be melted and reshaped, which answers the recycling problem of thermoset epoxies. Search for 'out-of-autoclave prepreg', 'resin infusion wind blade' and 'ceramic matrix composite turbine shroud' to go further.
